title: Geometry-Induced Domain-Wall Pinning and $\mathbb{Z}_2$ Asymmetry in Nominally One-Dimensional Rydberg Arrays
authors: Elijah Pelofske, Frank Barrows, Cristiano Nisoli
abstract: We perform experiments on QuEra's neutral-Rydberg-atom Aquila quantum computer, using quasi-adiabatic evolution on 1-dimensional models. We use hardware fine-tuning to balance the measurement statistics close to zero net magnetization, in two different geometric outlines: one closed triangular model with 33 atoms, and one 47-atom square with an engineered atom vacancy. The nature of this processor restricts the geometry of the atoms that can be programmed to a 2D plane. We report effects not predicted by the pure 1D Ising model, such as pinning of domain walls and $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry breaking due to the interplay between van der Waals interactions and the Rydberg blockade. In particular, atoms around the atom vacancy and at the vertices of the 1-dimensional square-outline model strongly prefer the Rydberg state, leading to the effective model having a ferromagnetic bond across the vacancy.
summary: The authors experimentally explore domain wall physics in Rydberg arrays using a neutral-atom quantum computer. By comparing closed triangular versus open square geometries, they demonstrate that geometric features like corners and vacancies induce strong local interactions. These effects lead to measurable symmetry breaking and pinning of topological defects, proving that the physical realization significantly modifies the underlying theoretical model.
main_problem: The study investigates how geometric constraints on a Rydberg array induce domain-wall pinning and break $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry in nominally one-dimensional quantum spin models.
main_result: The geometry dictates the physics, leading to non-uniform domain wall pinning at corners (triangle) or around engineered vacancies (square), and causing an observable imbalance favoring certain types of domain walls ($	ext{|gg}angle	ext{DWs}$ over $	ext{|rr}angle	ext{DWs}$).
method: The researchers used quasi-adiabatic evolution protocols on a neutral-Rydberg-atom quantum computer to sample the ground state configurations of an effective Ising-like Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The system is realized using QuEra's neutral-Rydberg-atom Aquila platform, simulating 1D chains (triangular and square outlines) governed by Rydberg blockade interactions ($V_{jk} \propto 1/r^6$).
key_observables: Domain wall number statistics (analyzed via Parity Biased Binomial distributions), site-resolved magnetization profiles, and the relative counts of different domain wall types ($	ext{|gg}angle$ vs $	ext{|rr}angle$).
important_parameters: The geometry (closed triangle vs. open square with vacancy) is critical; NNN interactions are significantly stronger at corners compared to edges.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system can be effectively modeled by an Ising-like Hamiltonian in a restricted subspace, and that finite-time ramping introduces non-adiabatic errors.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate atomic arrangements on the processor for both geometries; Figure 3 compares measured domain-wall statistics against theoretical distributions; Figures 4 and 5 map out site-resolved domain wall densities showing corner/vacancy effects.
paper_structure: The paper details experimental setups on two specific 1D geometries, analyzes domain-wall statistics using specialized distributions, and contrasts the observed pinning and symmetry breaking mechanisms between the closed (triangular) and open (square) boundaries.
why_interesting: This work provides direct experimental evidence of how engineered disorder or boundary conditions in quantum simulators can fundamentally alter the ground state properties and symmetries predicted by idealized 1D models, which is crucial for understanding real-world quantum hardware limitations.
